**Depreciation Schedule – 5‑Year Life, Cost $60 000, Salvage $10 000 (US GAAP)** | Year | Straight‑Line Expense | Accumulated Dep. SL | Book Value SL | Double‑Declining‑Balance (DDB) Expense | Accumulated Dep. DDB | Book Value DDB | |------|-----------------------|---------------------|---------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------|----------------| | 1 | **$10 000** | $10 000 | $50 000 | **$24 000** | $24 000 | $36 000 | | 2 | $10 000 | $20 000 | $40 000 | $14 400 | $38 400 | $21 600 | | 3 | $10 000 | $30 000 | $30 000 | $8 640 | $47 040 | $12 960 | | 4 | $10 000 | $40 000 | $20 000 | **$2 960** (switch to SL) | $50 000 | $10 000 | | 5 | $10 000 | $50 000 | $10 000 | $0 | $50 000 | $10 000 | *All amounts are in U.S. dollars.* ### How the numbers were derived 1. **Straight‑Line (SL)** * Depreciable base = Cost – Salvage = $60 000 – $10 000 = $50 000 * Annual expense = $50 000 ÷ 5 years = **$10 000** per year * Accumulated depreciation simply adds the yearly expense; book value is cost minus accumulated depreciation. 2. **Double‑Declining Balance (DDB)** – rate = 2 × (1/Useful life) = 40% * Year 1: $60 000 × 0.40 = **$24 000** → BV = $36 000 * Year 2: $36 000 × 0.40 = **$14 400** → BV = $21 600 * Year 3: $21 600 × 0.40 = **$8 640** → BV = $12 960 * Year 4: DDB would give $12 960 × 0.40 = $5 184, but that would drop the book value below the salvage of $10 000. The rule is to switch to straight‑line when the straight‑line expense for the remaining life exceeds the DDB expense **or** when the asset’s book value cannot fall below salvage. Remaining depreciable amount at start of Year 4 = $12 960 – $10 000 = $2 960, and only one year remains → straight‑line expense = **$2 960**. * Year 5: Book value equals salvage; no further depreciation. ### Expense patterns produced by each method | Method | Pattern of Expense | Why it occurs | |--------|--------------------|---------------| | Straight‑Line | Constant, equal amounts every year (except possibly the last if salvage ≠ 0) | Allocates cost evenly over the asset’s useful life; assumes uniform benefit or usage. | | Double‑Declining Balance (accelerated) | Large expense in early years, tapering to a small amount (or zero) later | Reflects that many assets provide most of their economic value early and become less productive or more obsolete as they age. | ### Why a company might prefer one method over the other | Preference | Typical Reason | |------------|----------------| | **Straight‑Line** | • Simplicity and predictability for financial reporting.
• Matches revenue when the asset’s contribution to sales is roughly constant.
• Preferred by investors who value consistent earnings. | | **Accelerated (DDB)** | • Provides larger tax deductions in the early years, reducing taxable income sooner (tax‑deferral benefit).
• Better matches expense with declining economic benefit or revenue when the asset’s productivity falls off quickly.
• Useful for assets that are likely to be replaced or become obsolete soon. | In practice, many companies use straight‑line for most assets but switch to an accelerated method (or vice versa) depending on tax strategy and how the asset’s value is expected to decline over time. The “switch to straight‑line when advantageous” rule ensures that depreciation never falls below salvage value while still capturing the benefits of acceleration early in the asset’s life.
